title: Why octopuses have three hearts
sources: Smithsonian Ocean: 'Octopuses: three hearts, blue blood'

verified.text: An octopus has three hearts: two branchial hearts and one systemic heart.
Each of the two branchial hearts pumps blood through one of the octopus's two gills.
The gills take up oxygen dissolved in the water that flows over them, so the blood picks up oxygen there.
The systemic heart then pumps the oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body, including the arms and the brain.
Octopus blood is blue because it carries oxygen with hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, instead of the iron-based hemoglobin in human blood.
The systemic heart stops beating while an octopus swims, which is one reason octopuses tire quickly when swimming and often crawl instead.
An octopus changes colour with chromatophores: tiny sacs of pigment in its skin that muscles stretch or squeeze, controlled by its nerves — not by its hearts or blood.

theories.text: Scientists think the extra hearts help because hemocyanin carries oxygen less efficiently than hemoglobin, so the blood needs an extra push through the gills.

knownErrors.correction: An octopus has three hearts: two branchial hearts (one per gill) and one systemic heart.

knownErrors.text: The hearts or blood make the octopus change colour
